vignette:
Dmitri Voss is a 37-year-old financial analyst of Polish-German descent who presents following eighteen months of progressively worsening post-traumatic symptoms stemming from a period of captivity he endured while traveling for work in a politically unstable region. He is recently divorced and lives alone in a two-bedroom apartment in a mid-sized American city. His PCL-5 score of 59 places him in the severe range, and he comes to the intake session neatly dressed but visibly strained, choosing a seat with his back against the wall and his eyes frequently moving toward the door.

Two years ago, Dmitri was detained by a paramilitary faction while attempting to reach a regional airport. He was held for eleven days in a windowless concrete room with two other captives he did not know. The conditions were deliberately disorienting - his captors cycled between long stretches of absolute silence and sudden, unpredictable intrusions involving shouting, physical handling, and threats. At several points the guards used what Dmitri now describes only as "techniques to remind us we were property." He was made to perform humiliating tasks on demand and was denied the ability to make any choices, however small, about his body or his time. The smell of mildew, unwashed clothing, and a particular brand of cheap cigarette smoke saturated those eleven days entirely. He was released after a ransom arrangement was negotiated by his employer, and none of the individuals responsible have ever been identified or charged. He returned to the United States physically intact but, in his own words, "fundamentally altered."

In the weeks after his return, Dmitri found himself unable to tolerate the ordinary textures of daily life. The first time a neighbor's child began crying in the hallway of his building, he pressed himself flat against his kitchen wall, heart slamming, certain that something was about to happen - though he could not have said what. That response has not diminished. In his open-plan office, the occasional sound of a colleague's child on a speakerphone call is enough to send him to the men's room for twenty minutes. He understands, intellectually, that a crying child is not a threat, but the sound reaches him somewhere older than understanding. Equally destabilizing is sudden silence. When a meeting room goes quiet, or when his apartment settles into complete stillness late at night, his body reads it as the particular loaded silence that preceded each intrusion during his captivity - the pause before the door opened. He has taken to sleeping with a podcast running, though even then he cannot fully relinquish alertness, lying awake monitoring the sounds of the building in a state of exhausting readiness.

Physical affection has become almost unbridictable. When his sister visited and reached to embrace him, he stepped back sharply before he could stop himself. He had come to associate the sensation of hands on his body with the loss of bodily autonomy he experienced during captivity, and a hug - however loving - carried in it the ghost of being handled without consent. His sister was hurt. His ex-wife had already noticed the withdrawal in the months before their divorce was finalized, describing him as "unreachable." He does not dispute this.

His memories of the eleven days are startlingly precise - more textured and immediate, he says, than memories of his own wedding or his daughter's birth. He can recall the exact grain of the concrete wall, the sequence of sounds before each intrusion. Occasionally, when the memories surface, he is briefly convinced he can smell the mildew and cigarettes, a sensory detail that makes the past feel less like memory and more like an ongoing condition.

What weighs on him most heavily, and what he returns to repeatedly in the intake session, is a cluster of beliefs about himself and the world that he cannot argue himself out of. He had acted during those eleven days in ways he finds deeply shameful - compliance, performance, things he believes no decent person would have done - and he is certain this reveals something irrevocable about his character. He feels, at a level beneath language, that he was reduced to an object, and that something of that objecthood has persisted. And the knowledge that the men responsible face no legal consequence anywhere in the world has left him with a corrosive sense that the moral order he once believed in was simply a story.

He sought help now, he says, because his twelve-year-old daughter asked to visit for the holidays and he realized he did not know how to let her hug him. That was the moment, he tells the therapist quietly, when he understood he could no longer manage this alone.
